input.question: If the Hubble telescope can zoom into the far reaches of the galaxy, why can't we just point it at Earth-like planets to see if they have water/vegetation etc.
input.ground_truth: We can't "see" earth like planets. They are too far away. The hubble telescope is great for seeing faint and far away things. We can see faint stars. We can see distant galaxies. We can see BOTH of these things because they give off light. We point our telescope at these and basically "leave the shutter open". This gathers light over an extended period of time. **Planets do not give off light. They only reflect light. This is not enough light to actually "see" the planet itself.** And on the remote chance we do see it, it isn't in enough detail to see the surface. The reason we know planets exist is not because we "see" them. It is because we see the effect they have on the stars they orbit.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a really, really powerful magnifying glass, like the Hubble telescope. This magnifying glass is amazing and can see things that are super, super far away—like stars and galaxies that are like grains of sand far, far away.

But if you want to look at a tiny, tiny ant on a rock that’s across the whole playground, even your super magnifying glass can’t see the ant’s details if the ant is too far away or too small. The Earth-like planets we want to look at are like those tiny ants—they are so far away in the sky that even Hubble can’t see if there are plants or water on them. It can only see if the planet is there and maybe if it’s a little bit round or bright, but not what’s on its surface.

To see if a planet has water or plants, we need a super, super powerful telescope or some special tricks, like watching if the planet passes in front of its star and seeing if the light changes in a way that tells us there might be something there. But Hubble just isn’t strong enough to see that much detail from so far away.
